title: Servant Leadership How to Lead Better by Getting Out of the Way
author: The Good Boss
summary: The Good Boss reframes leadership against the conventional spotlight model (own the room, set the vision, drive results) and argues that the most effective leaders he has worked with served, got out of the way, built trust instead of fear, and created space for others to grow. The piece traces servant leadership to Robert Greenleaf's 1970 coinage but notes the idea sits in much older philosophical and religious traditions of parenting and care. The mechanism is a flipped pyramid: instead of the leader at the top with instructions, pressure, and decisions flowing down, the leader sits at the bottom and support flows up to the team and through them to the customer. The leader's job becomes removing blockers, growing people, and creating an environment where the team can succeed; team growth becomes the leader's scoreboard. The shift is subtle but operationally consequential: from giving orders to asking 'how can I help?', from chasing credit to sharing it, from being the centre of every decision to building decision-makers. Servant leadership does not mean doing everyone's job or avoiding hard decisions; the leader's primary role is to build people, and durable team performance is the byproduct.
points: Servant leadership flips the question from 'how can my team help me succeed?' to 'how can I help my team succeed?' — which sounds soft but operationally redirects the leader's daily focus.
The pyramid is inverted: leader at the bottom, customer at the top, with support flowing up rather than orders flowing down; the leader's job becomes removing blockers and growing people.
The shifts are concrete: from giving orders to asking 'how can I help?', from chasing credit to sharing it, from being the centre of every decision to building decision-makers.
Servant leadership doesn't mean doing everyone's job or avoiding hard decisions; the primary role is to build people, and durable team performance follows.

The model has deep roots (Greenleaf 1970, plus older philosophical, religious, and parenting traditions) and works because supported team members feel motivated, take ownership, and solve bigger problems.
quotes: Most leadership advice is about being in the spotlight. You're told to own the room, set the vision, and drive results. You get praised for being in control, for being 'the expert', for always having the answers.
But what if that leadership advice is completely wrong? What if the best leaders don't take the spotlight, but instead… step back?
Servant Leadership flips the most fundamental element of leadership. Instead of asking, 'How can my team help me succeed?', a servant leader asks, 'How can I help my team succeed?'

Servant Leadership doesn't mean you do everyone's job. It doesn't mean you avoid hard decisions. It means your primary role as a leader is to build people. Their growth becomes your success. Their wins become your scoreboard.

Most managers default to control, and most leadership models work top-down. The leader sits at the top of the pyramid, followed by management, then employees, with the customer at the very bottom. Instructions, pressure, and decisions flow downward.

Servant leadership flips that pyramid. At the bottom is the leader, and at the very top is the customer. Instead of control flowing down, support flows up. Your job as a leader is no longer to command. It's to serve: to remove blockers, grow people, and create an environment where your team can succeed.” Archived from The Good Boss Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
